More than one hyphen, or a hyphen at either end

Neighbouring characters; safe because ends were rejected first
Punctuation that is not the final character

blocks.h: Why check a hyphen's position before looking at its neighbours?
p: For a hyphen at index 0, `w[i - 1]` would be `w[-1]` (the LAST character, because of Python's negative indexing) and for the last index `w[i + 1]` would raise `IndexError`. Rejecting hyphens at either end first makes the neighbour test safe. `-ab` and `ab-` are rejected for exactly that reason.

bullets: Time: O(n) over the characters of the sentence.
Space: O(n) for the token list.

2047.takeaway: Validate each token with simple character rules; reject boundary hyphens before indexing their neighbours.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Kahn's topological sort (BFS, Breadth-First Search, by in-degree)
A course can start only after ALL its prerequisites finish
Longest path to v so far, plus v's duration

p: n = 3, relations `[[1,3],[2,3]]`, time `[3,2,5]` → 8 (course 3 starts after both 1 and 2 end at months 3 and 2):

blocks.h: Why topological order with a max?
p: Courses run in parallel, so the finish time of a course is its own duration plus the LATEST finish among its prerequisites. That's the longest path (critical path) in the DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph). Processing nodes in topological order guarantees every prerequisite's finish is final before a node uses it.

2050.takeaway: Longest path in a DAG via Kahn's topological sort: finish[v] = time[v] + max finish of prerequisites.

bullets: Time: O(n²) worst case (a long vowel run).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Set of people who know the secret
Meetings at the same time form a graph where the secret can spread in any number of hops
Secrets only move forward in time
`deque(p for p in g if p in know)`
BFS (Breadth-First Search) sources: knowers who attend a meeting at this time
Only attendees can spread it now

blocks.h: Why group by time instead of processing meetings one by one?
p: Meetings at the same instant can pass the secret along a chain (A tells B, B tells C at the same time), regardless of the order of the list. Building a graph of one time's meetings and flooding from the knowers captures all such chains. Later times start from the updated `know` set. A person who learned the secret at time 8 can't have shared it at time 5.

bullets: Time: O(M log M) for sorting times plus O(M) per grouped search.

2092.takeaway: Process meetings by time: build that time's graph and BFS (Breadth-First Search) from current knowers, since same-time chains are instantaneous.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Single node: it is the middle
So that `slow` stops at the node BEFORE the middle
Singly linked delete needs its predecessor

blocks.h: Why does fast start at head.next.next?
p: If both started at the head, `slow` would end ON the middle node and we'd have no way to unlink it (no back pointer). Starting `fast` one step further ahead makes `slow` land on the predecessor of the middle. For 2 nodes: `fast` is `None`, so `slow` stays at the head and its next (the second node, the middle at index 1) is removed.

2095.takeaway: Slow/fast pointers with fast starting two nodes ahead stop slow just before the middle node, ready to unlink it.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Compare squares: no `sqrt` and no float errors
Directed edge: bomb i triggers bomb j
The relation is NOT symmetric: depends on i's radius only
Try each bomb as the first detonation
Counts bombs reachable by chain reaction

p: `[[2,1,3],[6,1,4]]` → 2 (distance² = 16; bomb 0 radius² = 9 does not reach bomb 1; bomb 1 radius² = 16 reaches bomb 0):

A big bomb can set off a small bomb that lies within its radius, while the small bomb's blast may not reach back. So edges are directed by the source bomb's radius. The answer is the largest set reachable from one start, found by a graph search from each node.

bullets: Time: O(n³): building the graph is O(n²), and a search from each of n starts costs up to O(n²).

2101.takeaway: Directed graph by blast radius, then a DFS (Depth-First Search) from each bomb to count the chain reaction.

p: `s = '))()))'`, `locked = '010100'` → True. Left-to-right (balance never negative):

The left-to-right pass proves every prefix can have at least as many '(' as ')' (turn all free characters into '('). That alone can still fail when too many '(' remain unclosed, which is detected by the mirrored pass (turn all free ones into ')' and scan from the right). Passing both, plus an even length, means a balanced assignment exists.

2116.takeaway: Two greedy passes: treat free characters as '(' left-to-right and as ')' right-to-left; the balance must never go negative (and length must be even).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Piece types differ only in allowed directions; a queen has both lists
The 'stay' move: the position at each second t = 0…7
A move is stored as the piece's position at every second
Moving k squares: position at second t, stopping after k seconds
Each piece moves one square per second and stops at its destination
Stop extending in a direction when leaving the board
Collects all destinations along each ray
Do two move-lists share a square at the same second?
`zip` aligns the two paths by time
Backtracking over pieces: choose one move for piece i, recurse, undo
Counts combinations where no pair ever collides

p: Results computed by running the code. 'Options' is how many moves (including staying) each piece has:

A rook at (1,1) moving 2 squares right is stored as its position at each second 0…7: [(1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 3), (1, 3), (1, 3), (1, 3), (1, 3)]. Two pieces collide only if the lists have equal entries at the same index, which also covers a piece waiting at its destination (it keeps its last position for the remaining seconds). Swapping places (crossing in the middle of a second) is allowed and not detected because only whole-second positions are compared.

At most 4 pieces, and each piece has at most 29 moves (queen), so at most 29⁴ ≈ 700,000 combinations, and backtracking prunes a combination as soon as the newest piece collides with an already chosen one.

bullets: Time: About O(moves^n · 8) for n ≤ 4 pieces.
Space: O(n · moves · 8) for the stored paths.

2056.takeaway: Represent each move as the piece's position at every second; backtrack over pieces and prune on same-square-same-time clashes.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Prune: only take an edge if there is time left
Bounds the DFS (Depth-First Search): each edge costs at least 10 time units in the original constraints, so paths are short
First time this path touches v
Only first visits add the node's value
Count visits along the CURRENT path, then undo
Backtracking; allows revisiting nodes without double counting
Only paths that are back at node 0 count
The path must start and end at 0

p: values `[0,32,10,43]`, edges `[[0,1,10],[1,2,15],[0,3,10]]`. Best quality for different time limits (computed): maxTime 49 → 75, 30 → 43, 20 → 43. Improving paths for 49 (as node sequences, time, quality):

blocks.h: Why DFS with a time budget, and why visit counts rather than a boolean?
p: The graph is tiny in degree (each node has at most 4 edges) and edges cost at least 10 with `maxTime ≤ 100`, so a path has at most 10 edges: DFS over all walks is feasible. A node may be visited several times on a walk (to get through) but its value must count once, so we keep a counter per node and add the value only when the counter goes 0 → 1; undoing the increment on return restores the state for other branches.

bullets: Time: Exponential in the number of edges on a walk (at most maxTime / minEdgeTime, about 10), roughly O(4^10).

2065.takeaway: DFS over walks bounded by maxTime; add a node's value only the first time it is visited on the current walk, and record the best when back at 0.

blocks.h: Why at most one centre word?
p: A palindrome has a single middle. Words like `gg` read the same reversed, so one unpaired copy can sit in the center and add 2 letters. Two leftover self-palindromic words can't both be central.

2131.takeaway: Pair each word with its reverse (4 letters per pair), pair up self-palindromic words, and add 2 if one is left over for the center.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of ones: the size of the block they must form
The final contiguous block has exactly w cells
Unrolls the circle: every circular window is an ordinary window in `t`
Each zero inside a window is a position that must receive a 1: one swap per zero
Slide: add the new cell's zero, drop the old cell's zero

blocks.h: Why does the number of zeros in a window give the swaps?
p: If the ones end up in a chosen window of length w, every 0 in that window must be swapped with a 1 outside it. The count of zeros inside equals the count of ones outside, so that many swaps are needed. We pick the window with the fewest zeros. Doubling the array handles windows that wrap around the circle's end.

2134.takeaway: Window of size = number of ones over the doubled array: the zeros inside the best window equal the swaps needed.

p: `nums1 = [1,2,5]`, `nums2 = [2,6,3]` → 3. Balances after each index (`balance: ways`):

blocks.h: Why track the difference instead of both sums?
p: Balanced means sum1 = sum2, which is the same as sum1 − sum2 = 0. Tracking only the difference needs one number per state instead of two. Every earlier state either extends with +a or −b, and the number of states is bounded by the total of the values (about 2·S).

bullets: Time: O(n · S) where S is the largest possible absolute difference (sum of the values).

2143.takeaway: DP over the difference sum1 − sum2: extend each balance by +a or −b, start new ranges, and count balance 0.

blocks.h: Why two write pointers instead of splitting into two lists?
p: Two lists would work too (collect positives, collect negatives, interleave) but need extra passes. Two write indexes place each number directly where it belongs in one pass; they never collide since there are equally many positives and negatives.

2149.takeaway: Two write indexes (even for positives, odd for negatives) place each number in one pass, keeping order within each sign.

p: `[[1,4],[4,7],[5,8]]` → [3, 3, 1]. The jump map after each day (unit cell → next candidate):

A naive solution marks each cell of the interval and re-scans already painted cells, which can be O(n) per day. The jump pointers let `find` skip a whole painted run in nearly constant time, so each cell is painted once and the total work is proportional to the painted area (times the inverse-Ackermann factor from path compression).

bullets: Time: About O(total painted length · α) plus the number of days.

2158.takeaway: Union-Find style jump pointers: find the next unpainted cell, paint it, and link it onward so painted runs are skipped.

blocks.h: Why three passes instead of an in-place partition?
p: An in-place swap-based partition (like quicksort's) doesn't preserve the relative order within groups. Building three lists with filters keeps each group's order (stability) at the cost of O(n) extra space and three scans.

2161.takeaway: Stable three-way partition: three filtered list comprehensions concatenated.

p: mapping `[8,9,4,0,2,1,3,5,7,6]`, nums `[991,338,38]` → [338, 38, 991] (338 and 38 both map to 7; their original order is kept):

The problem requires that numbers with equal mapped values stay in their original relative order. `sorted` is stable, so no tie-breaking key is needed. Using the index as an extra key would also work but is unnecessary.

bullets: Time: O(n log n + n·d) for d digits per number.

2191.takeaway: Sort by a key function that maps each digit; Python's stable sort keeps the original order for equal mapped values.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Two numbers are coprime iff the gcd is 1
What non-coprime neighbours are replaced by
The last number kept so far
The only neighbour a new number can interact with
Keep merging while the top shares a factor with the (growing) x
After a merge x changes, and may now share factors with the next stack element
Stack of numbers with no non-coprime neighbours

blocks.h: Why a stack and why does the order of merges not matter?
p: Merging only touches adjacent elements, and a merged number is compared again with the new top. A stack gives access to the left neighbour in O(1) and lets a merge cascade to the left (as with 6, 4, 3: 4 and 6 merge to 12, then 12 and 3 merge to 12). The final list is the same whichever adjacent non-coprime pair is merged first, so a left-to-right stack pass is valid.

bullets: Time: O(n log V): each push/pop pair costs a gcd (logarithmic in the values).

2197.takeaway: Stack with gcd/lcm: merge the incoming number with the top while they share a factor, then push.
